source_note: Steven M. LaValle, Planning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2006. Local file is the author's free electronic edition (planning.cs.uiuc.edu) as a single PDF of 13,370,045 bytes; full sha256 over (str(size) + bytes) is 03b0428ec0d05158092eb02cafc7e45c79dde7d89ea0516bcde0e080f7bed707, book_id is its first 16 hex characters. The extracted text (26,764 lines) is a two-column page layout; every verbatim quote was verified as a contiguous substring of that text file under the gatekeeper normalization. The work spans four parts (discrete planning, motion planning, decision-theoretic planning, planning under differential constraints), which is why the primitive count sits at the top of the fleet range. Motif-lane extraction (MOTIF-TIERB-DRAIN-01) of the same work for sync-cloud reconciliation.

primitives.name: Discrete feasible planning: a countable state space X, per-state action spaces U(x), a state transition function f with x' = f(x, u), an initial state, and a goal set (Formulation 2.1)
primitives.verbatim_quote: 3. A state transition function f that produces a state f (x, u) ∈ X for every

symbol_and_unit_ledger.x: current state, an element of the state space X
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x': successor state produced by applying u at x
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u: action drawn from U(x), the action space at x
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f: state transition function mapping (state, action) pairs to successor states

assumptions: The model is completely known and predictable; no uncertainty is present
X is finite or countably infinite and U(x) is finite for each x
The transition graph is usually specified implicitly and revealed incrementally, not enumerated in advance
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks when the state cannot be enumerated or compactly encoded: irrelevant information encoded into the state can convert a tractable problem into an intractable one, and continuous or uncertain problems need the extensions of Parts II-IV

layer2.mapping: This is the engine's root representation: a game situation is a state, a candidate decision is an action, and the simulator or learned dynamics that advance the situation are the transition function. Every higher layer in the book, and in the engine, is this same tuple with one complication added.
layer2.telemetry: State and event logs from play-by-play feeds, down, distance, field position, clock, score, and personnel groupings that instantiate X, U(x), and f

primitives.name: All search methods follow one template: incrementally grow a search graph G(V, E) inside the state transition graph by initializing, selecting a vertex, applying an action, inserting an edge, and checking for a solution
primitives.verbatim_quote: a search graph, G(V, E), which is the subgraph of the state transition graph that
assumptions: The transition graph is revealed incrementally through the application of actions instead of being fully specified in advance
The search is systematic: visited states are tracked so no redundant exploration occurs, and on infinite graphs every reachable vertex is reached in the limit
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails to terminate with a negative answer on infinite graphs when no solution exists, and the vertex-selection rule decides whether the search is complete, optimal, or merely fast

layer2.mapping: The engine's scenario exploration loop is this template: expand the most promising situation node, apply a candidate event or decision, record the edge and its cost, and stop when a goal region (a decision threshold) is encoded in the explored graph.
layer2.telemetry: Search telemetry: nodes expanded, edges generated, queue discipline, and time-to-solution per query

primitives.name: A* search: Dijkstra's algorithm with the priority C*(x) + G-hat*(x); if the heuristic G-hat*(x) underestimates the true optimal cost-to-go for every state, A* is guaranteed to find optimal plans
primitives.verbatim_quote: the optimal cost from xI to XG . If Ĝ∗ (x) is an underestimate of the true optimal

symbol_and_unit_ledger.G^{*}(x): true optimal cost-to-go from x to the goal set
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\hat{G}^{*}(x): heuristic estimate of the cost-to-go, required to be an underestimate
symbol_and_unit_ledger.C^{*}(x): optimal cost-to-come from the initial state to x

assumptions: An admissible (under)estimate of cost-to-go exists and is cheap to compute
Edge costs are nonnegative so Dijkstra's ordering argument applies
primitives.breakdown_regime: With an overestimating heuristic the optimality guarantee is lost; with the zero heuristic A* degenerates to Dijkstra and explores far more states, and a poor heuristic can be worse than none if it is expensive to evaluate

layer2.mapping: Any engine component that searches over situation trees can order its frontier by cost-so-far plus an admissible bound on cost-to-finish; the bound is what converts blind enumeration into directed search while keeping the final answer exact.
layer2.telemetry: Heuristic values per state, true realized cost-to-go from settled games, and node expansion counts to audit admissibility

primitives.name: Bidirectional search grows one tree from the initial state using f and one from the goal state using the backward transition function f-inverse, terminating when the trees meet
primitives.verbatim_quote: in Figures 2.4 and 2.6. One tree is grown from the initial state, and the other

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f^{-1}: backward state transition function yielding a predecessor state x from a successor x'
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u^{-1}: backward action drawn from the backward action space at x'
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x': successor state in the forward direction

assumptions: A single goal state (or small goal set) is given so the backward tree has a root
Predecessors under each action can be generated, which requires inverting the transition function
primitives.breakdown_regime: The two trees may pass close to each other without connecting, and for best-first variants ensuring an optimal meeting point is delicate; backward branching can exceed forward branching when f is many-to-one

layer2.mapping: Reasoning backward from a desired end state (a target score margin, a needed yardage outcome) while reasoning forward from the current situation halves the effective depth each side must cover when the branching factor is large.
layer2.telemetry: Forward and backward frontier sizes, meeting-node identity, and path cost stitched through the meeting point

primitives.name: Optimal planning adds a stage cost l(x, u) charged at every stage and a final cost l_F that is 0 on the goal set and infinity off it, so total plan cost is an additive functional over stages
primitives.verbatim_quote: The cost term l(xk , uk ) yields a real value for every xk ∈ X and uk ∈ U (xk ).

symbol_and_unit_ledger.l(x, u): real-valued cost charged for applying action u at state x
symbol_and_unit_ledger.l_F: final (terminal) cost function on the last state

assumptions: Costs are stage-additive: total cost is the sum of stage costs plus the final cost
Minimization is the convention; maximization is recovered by negating costs
primitives.breakdown_regime: Non-additive criteria (risk measures over whole trajectories, constraints coupling distant stages) do not fit the stage-cost form and block the dynamic programming decomposition

layer2.mapping: The engine scores candidate continuations with additive per-event costs (yards conceded, clock burned, injury risk incurred) plus a terminal term that is zero only inside the target outcome region; additivity is exactly what makes the total decomposable stage by stage.
layer2.telemetry: Per-event cost components from game logs, terminal outcome labels, and the realized sum along completed trajectories

primitives.name: Principle of optimality: portions of optimal plans are themselves optimal, so an optimal plan can be built by composing optimal suffixes
primitives.verbatim_quote: optimal. It would be absurd to be able to replace a portion of an optimal plan
assumptions: The cost functional is stage-additive and the future cost depends on the past only through the current state
The problem is stated so that a suffix of a plan is itself a plan for the subproblem starting at the intermediate state
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when the objective couples stages non-additively or when hidden state makes the current state an insufficient summary of the past; then suffixes of optimal plans need not be optimal

layer2.mapping: This is the license for the engine to cache and reuse evaluated continuations: if the best continuation from a situation is computed once, it can be spliced into every larger analysis that passes through that situation.
layer2.telemetry: Situation identifiers, cached continuation values, and reuse counts across analyses

primitives.name: Backward value iteration computes optimal cost-to-go functions stage by stage: G*_k is obtained from G*_{k+1} by minimizing stage cost plus the cost-to-go of the successor (equation 2.7 family)
primitives.verbatim_quote: G∗k (xk ) = min l(xk , uk ) + G∗k+1 (xk+1 ) ,
primitives.latex: G^{*}_k(x_k) = \min_{u_k \in U(x_k)} \left[ l(x_k, u_k) + G^{*}_{k+1}\left(f(x_k, u_k)\right) \right]

symbol_and_unit_ledger.G^{*}_k(x_k): optimal cost-to-go from state x_k at stage k
symbol_and_unit_ledger.K: fixed number of stages in the plan

assumptions: The plan length K is fixed and the final cost G*_F = l_F is known
Each iteration costs O(|X||U|) time, giving O(K|X||U|) overall
primitives.breakdown_regime: Useless when |X| is huge or continuous without approximation, and a naive enumeration of action sequences would cost O(|U|^K); the fixed-length case alone does not handle plans of unknown length

layer2.mapping: The engine's finite-horizon evaluator is this recursion: with a fixed number of remaining events (plays, possessions, minutes), value is backed up from terminal outcomes through the situation graph one stage at a time.
layer2.telemetry: Remaining-stage counts, per-stage costs, successor distributions from the situation model, and backed-up values per stage

primitives.name: For variable-length plans the iteration reaches a stationary optimal cost-to-go G* satisfying the fixed-point equation, and the optimal feedback plan is recovered by a local operator u* = argmin over actions of stage cost plus G* of the successor
primitives.verbatim_quote: value G∗ (x) gives the optimal cost to go from state x ∈ X to the speciﬁc goal state
primitives.latex: G^{*}(x) = \min_{u \in U(x)} \left[ l(x, u) + G^{*}\left(f(x, u)\right) \right]

symbol_and_unit_ledger.G^{*}(x): stationary optimal cost-to-go from state x, independent of stage index
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u^{*}: optimal action recovered from G* by the local operator

assumptions: A termination action exists so plans can end, and costs are positive off the goal so the fixed point is well defined
Value iteration is run until successive functions agree on every state
primitives.breakdown_regime: If zero-cost cycles exist the iteration may not settle to the intended fixed point; the cost-to-go alone does not store the plan, so actions must be re-derived by the local operator at execution time

layer2.mapping: A single value function over situations, plus a greedy local operator, is a complete decision policy: the engine can store one number per situation class and regenerate the recommended decision on demand instead of storing decision tables.
layer2.telemetry: Value function snapshots, local-operator decisions per situation, and realized costs of executed decisions

primitives.name: Configuration space (C-space): if a robot has n degrees of freedom, the set of its transformations is a manifold of dimension n, and motion planning becomes path computation on that manifold; a 2D rigid body has C = R^2 x S^1 and a 3D rigid body has C = R^3 x RP^3
primitives.verbatim_quote: manifold of dimension n. This manifold is called the configuration space of the

symbol_and_unit_ledger.C: configuration space, the manifold of all configurations
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\mathbb{R}^2: translations of the body in the plane
symbol_and_unit_ledger.S^1: orientations of the body, with angle 0 identified with 2 pi
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n: number of degrees of freedom, equal to the dimension of C

assumptions: The robot's transformations form a smooth manifold whose dimension equals the degrees of freedom
Topology must be respected: angles wrap around, so S^1 rather than R is the orientation factor
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks as a naive vector-space picture: C is generally not R^n, distances and neighborhoods are manifold notions, and closed kinematic chains cut C down to complicated submanifolds

layer2.mapping: The engine's situation space is the same move: replace a complicated physical description (players, formations, field geometry) with one point in an abstract state manifold, then let every algorithm work on points and paths in that space.
layer2.telemetry: Situation embeddings, the dimension and topology of the situation representation, and coverage of the manifold by observed games

primitives.name: Configuration-space obstacle: Cobs is the set of configurations at which the placed robot intersects the obstacle region, and Cfree is its complement; planning is a path problem in Cfree
primitives.verbatim_quote: The obstacle region, Cobs ⊆ C, is deﬁned as

symbol_and_unit_ledger.A(q): the subset of the workspace occupied by the robot at configuration q
symbol_and_unit_ledger.C_{free}: complement of Cobs in C, the free configuration space

assumptions: Robot and obstacle are semi-algebraic (polygonal or polyhedral) models in a 2D or 3D workspace
A(q) is obtained from a reference placement by the transformation q
primitives.breakdown_regime: Explicitly constructing the boundary of Cobs is usually impractical in high dimensions, which is why sampling-based methods only test membership (collision checking) instead of building Cobs

layer2.mapping: Forbidden regions of situation space (lineups ruled out by injury, formations illegal under the rules, matchups already refuted by evidence) are Cobs: the engine needs a membership test, not an explicit map of the forbidden set, to plan around them.
layer2.telemetry: Membership-test outcomes per candidate situation, constraint violations logged, and the sampled fraction of forbidden space

primitives.name: For a translating rigid robot the C-space obstacle is a Minkowski difference of workspace sets, Cobs = O minus A(0), with X minus Y defined as all pairwise vector differences
primitives.verbatim_quote: X, Y ⊂ Rn , let their Minkowski difference10 be deﬁned as
primitives.latex: X \ominus Y = \{ x - y \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid x \in X \text{ and } y \in Y \}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.X, Y: subsets of R^n (obstacle region and negated robot shape)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.A(0): robot placed at the reference configuration

assumptions: The robot is restricted to translation only, so C = R^n
Robot and obstacle are given as explicit sets in the same workspace coordinates
primitives.breakdown_regime: Only the translational case has this clean form; with rotation the C-obstacle is a union of slices, and for convex polygons the construction reduces to sorting edge normals (the star algorithm), while nonconvex shapes must be decomposed into convex parts

layer2.mapping: Growing a forbidden region by the shape of the thing that must avoid it is a reusable operation: inflate a constraint set by the footprint of a candidate plan and feasibility becomes a point-membership test.
layer2.telemetry: Set representations of constraints and candidate footprints, and inflated-region membership results

primitives.name: The basic motion planning problem (Formulation 4.1, the Piano Mover's Problem) asks for a continuous path in Cfree between query configurations or a correct report that none exists, and it is PSPACE-hard (Reif)
primitives.verbatim_quote: It was shown by Reif [817] that this problem is PSPACE-hard, which implies
assumptions: A complete algorithm must either produce the path or correctly report that none exists
Robot and obstacles are semi-algebraic so the problem is decidable in principle
primitives.breakdown_regime: PSPACE-hardness in the dimension of C kills any hope of a general polynomial complete algorithm; practical complete methods are exponential, which motivates sampling-based planners that trade completeness for probabilistic or resolution variants

layer2.mapping: A standing warning for the engine: exact, complete reasoning over the full situation space is intractable in the worst case, so guarantees must be bought deliberately (restricted subspaces, sampling, or bounded horizons) rather than assumed.
layer2.telemetry: Problem size (state dimension, branching), solver run times, and which guarantee class each engine component actually provides

primitives.name: Dispersion of a sample set P in a metric space (X, rho) is the radius of the largest empty ball; minimizing dispersion generalizes grid resolution, and any k samples in [0,1]^n have dispersion at least (1/2) k^(-1/n)
primitives.verbatim_quote: An alternative way to consider dispersion is as the radius of the largest empty

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\delta(P): dispersion of the sample set P
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\rho(x, p): metric distance between a point x and a sample p
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P: finite set of samples in X
symbol_and_unit_ledger.sup: supremum, the least upper bound over all x in X

assumptions: A metric on the configuration space is fixed in advance
Lower dispersion is better, despite the name; the Sukharev grid attains the optimal bound for the L-infinity metric
primitives.breakdown_regime: Keeping dispersion fixed requires exponentially many points as dimension grows, and optimizing L2 dispersion is unsolved even in moderate dimensions; uniform random samples leave irregular holes that dispersion-optimal deterministic sequences avoid but at the cost of statistical randomness

layer2.mapping: Dispersion is the engine's coverage metric for scenario sampling: the worst-case distance from any possible game situation to the nearest simulated or historical situation bounds how wrong an interpolated evaluation can be.
layer2.telemetry: Sample sets over situation space, nearest-neighbor distances, and the largest uncovered region radius per analysis

primitives.name: Sampling-based planners are probabilistically complete: with enough samples the probability of finding a solution, when one exists, approaches one, without a finite-time guarantee
primitives.verbatim_quote: to algorithms that are probabilistically complete, which means that with enough
assumptions: The sampling sequence is dense in the free space (with probability one for random sequences)
A solution path exists with some clearance from obstacles so samples can approximate it
primitives.breakdown_regime: No finite sample bound is given: narrow passages with tiny volume are found only after enormous sampling, and failure to find a path never proves that none exists

layer2.mapping: Monte Carlo components of the engine inherit exactly this guarantee shape: more simulations monotonically raise the chance of discovering a viable line of play, but a null result is evidence, never proof, of impossibility.
layer2.telemetry: Simulation counts, discovery rates as a function of sample count, and clearance margins of found solutions

primitives.name: General sampling-based planning framework: each iteration applies a vertex selection method (VSM) to pick a graph vertex to expand and a local planning method (LPM) to generate a new configuration toward which an edge is attempted
primitives.verbatim_quote: convenience, step 2 will be called the vertex selection method (VSM) and step 3
assumptions: Collision checking is available as a black box; Cobs is never explicitly constructed
Sampling and searching are interleaved so resolution is refined only until a solution is found
primitives.breakdown_regime: Heuristic members of the family (randomized potential fields) depend on problem-specific parameter tuning and can stall in local minima; the framework itself gives no completeness until the VSM and sampling sequence are specified

layer2.mapping: This is the engine's simulation loop abstracted: a selection rule decides which evaluated situation to extend, and a local generator proposes the next event; swapping either rule changes the planner without changing the surrounding machinery.
layer2.telemetry: Selection frequencies per vertex class, local generation success rates, and edges added per iteration

primitives.name: Rapidly exploring dense trees (RDTs, with RRTs as the random case): given a dense sequence alpha, iteratively connect each alpha(i) to the nearest point of the tree's swath, so the tree is dense in the free space in the limit
primitives.verbatim_quote: dense sequence, α, and iteratively connects from α(i) to the nearest point among
assumptions: The guiding sequence alpha is dense in C (random sequences are dense with probability one)
A nearest-point query over the swath of the tree and a local connection path are available; with obstacles the edge stops at the collision boundary
primitives.breakdown_regime: The tree is not optimal: first-found paths can be far from shortest, the metric used for nearest queries biases growth, and performance depends on the sampling distribution matching the problem's narrow regions

layer2.mapping: Growing a tree of game continuations by always extending toward the nearest unexplored region of situation space gives the engine an exploration strategy that provably fills the space instead of re-sampling the same likely lines.
layer2.telemetry: Tree size, nearest-neighbor distances per iteration, and the fraction of situation space within a fixed radius of the tree

primitives.name: Sampling-based roadmaps (PRMs) incrementally build a graph by connecting each new sample to nearby vertices, producing a reusable roadmap that answers many initial-goal queries
primitives.verbatim_quote: roadmap, which eﬃciently solves multiple initial-goal queries. Intuitively, the paths
assumptions: Many queries share the same static free space, so preprocessing cost is amortized
A local planner can connect nearby configurations with simple paths, and connection radius or neighbor count is chosen to keep the graph connected
primitives.breakdown_regime: Roadmaps are wasteful for a single query and degrade when the environment changes between queries; connection attempts dominate cost and most fail in cluttered regions

layer2.mapping: Precompute a graph of reachable situation transitions once, then answer many what-if queries by connecting the query endpoints to the graph; the engine reuses one expensive structure across all of a week's analyses.
layer2.telemetry: Roadmap vertex and edge counts, query connection success, and reuse counts per query

primitives.name: Combinatorial planning by cell decomposition: partition Cfree into finitely many cells (for example trapezoidal cells from vertical slices at obstacle vertices), put a sample point in each cell, and search the resulting adjacency roadmap
primitives.verbatim_quote: this partitioning of Cf ree into a ﬁnite set of regions called cells. The term k-
assumptions: Obstacles are polygonal and in general position (no two vertices share a vertical line) for the basic vertical decomposition
Inside a cell any two points connect trivially, for example by a line segment in a convex cell, so connectivity of the roadmap matches connectivity of Cfree
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exact decompositions explode combinatorially in higher dimensions and for algebraic obstacles require cylindrical algebraic decomposition; degenerate configurations violate general position and dominate implementation effort

layer2.mapping: Partitioning a continuous evaluation space into finitely many cells inside which the answer is uniform converts a continuous problem into a graph problem; the engine does the same when it buckets situations into classes that share one evaluation.
layer2.telemetry: Cell definitions, per-cell sample representatives, adjacency edges, and within-cell outcome variance as the audit of the partition

primitives.name: A potential function phi is a (feasible) navigation function if phi is zero exactly on the goal set, infinite exactly where the goal is unreachable, and strictly decreased by the local operator from every other reachable state; Dijkstra or wavefront propagation from the goal computes one
primitives.verbatim_quote: potential function, φ, is called a (feasible) navigation function if

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\varphi: potential (navigation) function from states to [0, infinity]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u^{*}: action selected by the local operator

assumptions: The cost functional is isotropic for the simplest form, so the stage cost drops out of the local operator
A navigation function and a feedback plan are interchangeable representations: each can be recovered from the other
primitives.breakdown_regime: Arbitrary potentials create local minima and cycles; only functions satisfying the three conditions guarantee arrival, and in continuous spaces smooth navigation functions may fail to exist on topologically complicated domains

layer2.mapping: A scalar field over situations with no spurious local minima turns evaluation into control: always move to the reachable situation with the lowest field value. The engine's win-probability-style surfaces play this role and must be audited for local minima that trap greedy reasoning.
layer2.telemetry: Potential values per situation, descent success rate under the local operator, and counts of states where no descending action exists

primitives.name: Bayes' rule converts a likelihood and a prior into a posterior by swapping the conditioned events and normalizing by marginalization
primitives.verbatim_quote: which nicely relates P (E|F ) to P (F |E). This results in Bayes’ rule, which is a

symbol_and_unit_ledger.P(F): prior probability of F, assessed before E is considered
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P(F \\mid E): posterior probability of F after E is considered
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P(E \\mid F): likelihood of the evidence E given F
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P(E): marginal probability of the evidence, obtained by marginalization over a partition

assumptions: The prior is specified before seeing the evidence and the likelihood model is trusted
The denominator is computed by marginalization over a partition of the sample space
primitives.breakdown_regime: Garbage priors give garbage posteriors: with little data the prior dominates, and the rule says nothing about where the prior or likelihood should come from (the Bayesian-frequentist dispute of Section 9.5)

layer2.mapping: Every belief update in the engine is this swap: prior belief about a hidden condition, likelihood of the observed event under each condition, posterior out. It is the single update rule behind the information-state filters of Chapter 11.
layer2.telemetry: Priors per hypothesis, likelihoods per observation type, and posterior trajectories over a game or season

primitives.name: The expectation of a random variable is its probability-weighted average over the sample space, and conditional expectation restricts the average to trials satisfying a given event
primitives.verbatim_quote: noted by E[X]. It can be considered as a kind of weighted average for X, in which

symbol_and_unit_ledger.X: random variable, a function from the sample space S to the reals

assumptions: The sample space is discrete for the sum form; the continuous case replaces the sum with an integral
The expected value need not be an attainable value of X
primitives.breakdown_regime: Expectation collapses a distribution to one number, hiding variance and tail risk; decisions that are right on average can be unacceptable when a single trial matters

layer2.mapping: Expected value is the engine's default scoring functional for uncertain continuations: average the outcome measure over the outcome distribution instead of planning against one guessed outcome.
layer2.telemetry: Outcome distributions per situation, expected values, and the spread around them for risk reporting

primitives.name: Game against nature, nondeterministic model: with no probabilities over nature's actions, choose the action minimizing the worst-case cost (minimax, equation 9.14)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The action u is the lowest cost choice using worst-case analysis. This is sometimes

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\theta: nature's action, from the set Theta
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L(u, \\theta): cost incurred when action u meets nature action theta

assumptions: Nature is modeled nondeterministically: every theta in Theta is possible and none is more likely
Costs for all action pairs fit in a |U| by |Theta| cost matrix when both sets are finite
primitives.breakdown_regime: Worst-case analysis is pessimistic: it ignores all frequency information, and if Theta is misspecified to include impossible nature actions the chosen action can be needlessly conservative; with infinite sets min and max become inf and sup and may not be attained

layer2.mapping: When the engine has no defensible distribution over an opponent's or environment's response, the minimax criterion is the honest fallback: pick the decision whose worst plausible consequence is least bad, and record that the choice was distribution-free.
layer2.telemetry: Candidate decisions, enumerated response sets, worst-case cost per decision, and the identity of the binding worst case

primitives.name: Game against nature, probabilistic model: when nature's distribution P(theta) is reliably estimated, choose the action minimizing expected cost (equation 9.15); the best action genuinely depends on the distribution
primitives.verbatim_quote: This involves computing the expected cost for each action:

symbol_and_unit_ledger.E_{\\theta}: expectation taken over nature's action distribution P(theta)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L(u, \\theta): cost of action u under nature action theta
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P(\\theta): estimated probability distribution over nature's actions

assumptions: Enough independent trials have been observed to estimate P(theta) reliably, and nature does not adapt its distribution in response to the decision maker
primitives.breakdown_regime: If the estimated distribution is wrong, expected-cost decisions can be worse than minimax ones; assigning a uniform distribution in the absence of data is explicitly flagged as dangerous

layer2.mapping: This is the engine's standard decision rule once response frequencies are measured: weight each response's cost by its observed probability and take the minimum, with the estimate's sample size carried alongside the decision.
layer2.telemetry: Response frequency tables, expected cost per candidate decision, and estimation sample sizes

primitives.name: Regret of an action under a nature action is the excess cost over the best action for that nature action; decisions can be made by minimizing worst-case or expected regret instead of cost (equations 9.17-9.22)
primitives.verbatim_quote: of cost that you could have saved by picking a diﬀerent action, given the nature

symbol_and_unit_ledger.T(u, \\theta): regret of action u when nature plays theta
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L(u', \\theta): cost of an alternative action u' under the same nature action

assumptions: Regret is computed after the fact against the best response to the realized nature action
The regret matrix has the same dimensions as the cost matrix
primitives.breakdown_regime: Regret-optimal actions differ from cost-optimal ones and can sacrifice absolute performance to avoid embarrassment; regret also depends on which alternatives are included in U, so adding a dominated action can change regrets

layer2.mapping: Post-hoc grading of engine decisions uses regret: compare the chosen line's realized cost with the best line available under what actually happened, separating decision quality from outcome luck.
layer2.telemetry: Chosen actions, realized conditions, best-response costs per realized condition, and regret per decision

primitives.name: Two-player zero-sum games: randomized (security) strategies are computed from the upper and lower envelopes of linear functions, equivalently by linear programming, and the randomized saddle value makes the min and max commute
primitives.verbatim_quote: for z2 = 1. The lines are plotted in Figure 9.4a. The security strategy is determined
primitives.latex: \min_{w \in W} \max_{z \in Z} \bar{L}(w, z) = \max_{z \in Z} \min_{w \in W} \bar{L}(w, z)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.w, z: randomized strategies (probability distributions over actions) for players P1 and P2
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\bar{L}(w, z): expected cost under the pair of randomized strategies
symbol_and_unit_ledger.W, Z: sets of all randomized strategies for the two players

assumptions: The game is zero-sum with a finite cost matrix, and both players may randomize independently at each play
Deterministic strategies suffice for the opponent's best response once one side's mixture is fixed, because the expected cost is linear in each mixture
primitives.breakdown_regime: Against a non-adversarial nature randomization gains nothing (a deterministic best action is already optimal); computing equilibria in high dimensions is a linear program whose cost grows quickly, and repeated-play learning by the opponent is the real justification for mixing

layer2.mapping: When an opponent can learn a deterministic tendency, the engine should evaluate mixed strategies: a distribution over decisions whose expected cost is guaranteed regardless of the response, computed by the same envelope or linear-programming machinery.
layer2.telemetry: Mixture weights per decision, expected cost against best response, and opponent tendency estimates from repeated matchups

primitives.name: In a two-player nonzero-sum game, a pair of actions is a Nash equilibrium when each player's action minimizes its own cost given the other's action, so neither player has regret (equations 9.66-9.67)
primitives.verbatim_quote: These expressions imply that neither P1 nor P2 has regret.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_1, L_2: independent cost functions of players P1 and P2
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u^{*}, v^{*}: the equilibrium actions of P1 and P2

layer2.mapping: The engine never sees the true game state directly; it sees a history of events and reports. Treating that history itself as the state, and policies as functions of it, is the correct formal frame for every partially observed evaluation.

primitives.name: A system x-dot = f(x, u) is controllable if every goal state lies in the reachable set of every initial state; it is small-time locally controllable if reachable sets contain neighborhoods of the initial state over arbitrarily small times, the property that lets sampling planners replace trajectory segments locally

layer2.mapping: Before optimizing, the engine should ask the controllability question of its own decision models: from any current situation, can the target class of situations be reached at all by allowed decisions, and can small corrections be made locally without a global replan.
layer2.telemetry: Reachability audits between situation classes, local correction success rates, and lists of situation pairs with no connecting decision sequence

reasoning_traces.think:
This book is built on a single representational decision that everything else inherits: a planning problem is a state space, an action space, a transition function, and a criterion, and a plan is either a sequence of actions or a feedback rule that maps states to actions. Part I states the idea in its purest form. Formulation 2.1 defines discrete feasible planning with the transition equation x' = f(x, u), and Chapter 2 then shows that graph search, Dijkstra, A-star, and dynamic programming are all manipulations of that one object. The search template of Section 2.2.4, in which a graph is grown inside the state transition graph by selecting vertices and applying actions, turns out to be the skeleton key for the entire book: sampling-based motion planning, reachability analysis, and even information-space planning are later presented as the same template with different state spaces and different vertex selection rules. Value iteration is the second pillar. The principle of optimality converts an exponential enumeration of action sequences into a recursion over cost-to-go functions, and the stationary form of that recursion shows that a single function G-star, plus a greedy local operator, is a complete representation of an optimal feedback plan. That identification, value function equals plan, recurs in every part: navigation functions in Chapter 8, cost-to-go in Chapter 10, and the HJB equation in Chapter 15 are the same object at different levels of continuity and uncertainty.

Part II asks what happens when the state space is a manifold instead of a graph. The configuration space construction converts a physical robot into a point in a space whose dimension is the number of degrees of freedom, and Cobs converts collision into set membership. Once that abstraction is accepted, the algorithmic question splits into two families that the book keeps in permanent tension. Combinatorial methods, such as cell decompositions and roadmaps, construct a finite structure that exactly captures the connectivity of the free space, and they inherit exactness at exponential cost; the PSPACE-hardness of the piano mover's problem explains why that cost cannot be removed in general. Sampling-based methods give up exactness and instead control coverage, through dispersion, dense sequences, and probabilistic completeness. The rapidly exploring dense tree is the emblematic construction: a dense sequence of samples plus a nearest-point connection rule produces a tree that fills the space, and the analysis of why it works is topological rather than combinatorial.

Two refinements of the discrete theory deserve emphasis because later chapters lean on them. First, the cost-to-go formulation quietly changes what a plan is: instead of an open-loop sequence of actions, the deliverable becomes a feedback plan, a function from states to actions that reacts to wherever execution actually arrives, and the local operator shows the two representations are interchangeable once G-star is known. Second, the treatment of search is deliberately unified: breadth-first, Dijkstra, A-star, and value iteration differ only in the order in which vertices are settled and in whether costs are attached to edges, so the book can prove optimality once for the family rather than once per algorithm. Chapter 8 then closes Part II's arc by observing that a navigation function is exactly a cost-to-go function for a continuous problem, and that wavefront propagation is Dijkstra's algorithm wearing a continuous disguise.

Part III adds uncertainty in two grades. Chapter 9 isolates the one-stage decision: Bayes' rule for updating beliefs, expectation for averaging, minimax for distribution-free choice, regret as an alternative currency, and Nash equilibrium when the uncertainty is another decision maker. Chapter 10 chains the one-stage problem with the dynamic programming machinery of Chapter 2, replacing the deterministic successor with a transition distribution and the recursion with its probabilistic analog; policy iteration and Q-learning then show that the same fixed point can be reached by searching in plan space or by simulation when the model is unknown. Chapter 11 makes the deepest move in the book: when the state itself is hidden, the history of actions and observations becomes the state, and planning is lifted to an information space. The derived information states, the set-valued nondeterministic filter and the probabilistic Bayes filter, are sufficient statistics that compress the history, and they are exact analogs of each other with union and intersection replaced by marginalization and Bayes' rule. Part IV finally adds differential constraints: the transition function becomes a vector field, configurations acquire velocities, nonholonomic constraints restrict instantaneous motion without restricting reachable configurations, and the discrete dynamic programming recursion passes to its continuous limit as the HJB equation.

For a reasoning engine, the transferable content is the discipline of the formalism. Every capability in the book is a tuple: a state representation, a transition model, an observation model if the state is hidden, a cost functional, and a guarantee class that states precisely what the method promises (complete, resolution complete, probabilistically complete, optimal, or merely feasible). The book is relentless about naming the guarantee and the assumption that buys it, which is what makes its machinery safe to reuse. Its limits are equally explicit. Exact methods die by dimension: cell decompositions, power-set information spaces, and grids all explode, and dispersion quantifies the explosion for sampling. Value iteration is linear in the state space per sweep, which is fatal when states are situations in a rich domain unless function approximation enters, and the book only gestures at that through simulation-based updates. The information space is uncountable even for finite state spaces once beliefs are distributions. The correct way to use the book is therefore not as a catalog of algorithms to run verbatim, but as a grammar: pick the state space honestly, state the transition and observation models, choose the weakest guarantee that the application can live with, and let the formalism show which algorithm family that choice forces.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The genealogy runs through four traditions that were separate before this book fused them. From artificial intelligence comes STRIPS-style discrete planning and graph search, with Dijkstra and A-star as the algorithmic core. From robotics comes the configuration space, introduced by Lozano-Perez, and the piano mover's problem whose PSPACE-hardness Reif established, which together forced the field to choose between exact combinatorial geometry and sampling. From control theory comes dynamic programming in the line of Bellman, feedback plans, controllability, and the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, with Pontryagin's minimum principle as its sibling. From decision theory and game theory come Bayes' rule as an update discipline, von Neumann's minimax and randomized security strategies, and Nash equilibrium. LaValle's contribution is not a new algorithm so much as a translation scheme: each tradition's central object is shown to be the same state-space tuple viewed at a different level of continuity, uncertainty, or differentiability, so results proved in one dialect, such as value iteration, can be carried into the others.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The author's model of the reader is a technically literate builder who will implement these methods, so the book privileges definitions that can be coded: every concept arrives as a formulation with numbered components, an algorithm template, and a stated guarantee. His model of the domain is that planning is one subject, not four: he refuses the historical split in which planning means logic to AI researchers, geometry to roboticists, and feedback to control theorists, and he treats the terminological differences (robot, agent, controller, player) as interchangeable labels for a decision maker. He also believes feasibility precedes optimality and that a method's assumptions are part of the method: nearly every chapter pauses to state what breaks the construction, from general position in cell decompositions to the danger of inventing a uniform prior. The reader is expected to share this discipline and to distrust any planner whose guarantee class is unnamed.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Several results in the book veto design choices that other layers might prefer. PSPACE-hardness vetoes any promise of exact, complete planning in unrestricted configuration spaces, so higher layers must budget for sampling or restriction. The dispersion lower bound vetoes cheap coverage: any layer that claims uniform evaluation quality over a d-dimensional situation space owes exponentially many samples in d, or must lower the claim. The navigation function conditions veto greedy use of arbitrary value surfaces: if the surface has a local minimum off the goal, greedy descent is not a plan, no matter how good the surface's predictions are. The information-space construction vetoes acting as if the state were known when only observations are available; decisions must be functions of the information state. Finally, the discussion of priors vetoes fabricated distributions: where no frequencies exist, the book's own machinery prescribes minimax, not an invented uniform distribution dressed as knowledge.

universal_lens: Any problem of choosing actions over time can be forced into one grammar: name the state space, the transition law, what is observed, what each step costs, and what guarantee is required. Once stated in that grammar, the problem inherits a century of machinery: search if the space is a graph, sampling if it is a manifold, dynamic programming if costs are additive, belief filtering if the state is hidden, and optimal control if the dynamics are differential. The grammar also exposes dishonesty: a method that cannot name its state space or its guarantee class is not yet a method.
gsi_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Institute, the book is a curriculum in formal decision science: it teaches how to state an evaluation problem precisely, how completeness and optimality guarantees are bought with assumptions, and how uncertainty changes the object being planned over from states to information states. Its four-part escalation, from discrete search to belief-space planning under differential constraints, is a ready-made syllabus for training analysts to recognize which formal problem they are actually solving before they reach for a technique.
gse_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Edge engine, the book supplies the operating formalism of the prediction and reasoning core: situations as states, candidate decisions as actions, a transition model over game sequences, additive stage costs, value functions whose greedy local operator yields decisions, and belief-state filters for hidden conditions such as health and opponent tendencies. Its guarantee discipline also governs the engine's honesty: every component must declare whether it is exact, sampled, or heuristic, and what assumption buys that status.
